# Macchuddānajātaka (Ja 288)

**ID:** Ja 288  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Macchuddānajātaka

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Macchuddānajātaka* (Ja 288) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Jātaka* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya. The story of the present is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivered the teaching concerning a dishonest merchant (*kūṭavāṇija*), opening with the verse beginning *agghanti macchā* [Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of landholders (*kuṭimbikakula*) during the reign of Brahmadatta in Bārāṇasī [Fausböll 1879]. While waiting with his brother on the banks of the Ganges for a boat, they ate a meal; the Bodhisatta cast the leftover food into the river for the fish and formally dedicated the merit or spiritual profit (*patti*) to the river spirit, who twice derived immediate benefit from the gift [O'Flaherty 1980]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha revealed that the dishonest merchant was the younger brother of that time, while he himself was the elder brother, with the merchant subsequently establishing himself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*) [Fausböll 1879].

**Sources**

- [Fausböll 1879] V. Fausböll, Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 2 (1879) — Pali text of the opening and closing verses, setting at Jetavana, past rebirth details, alternative title, and samodhāna.
- [O'Flaherty 1980] Wendy Doniger O'Flaherty, ed., Karma and Rebirth in Classical Indian Traditions (1980) — Account of the narrative theme involving feeding the fish, sharing merit (patti) with the river spirit, and doctrinal significance.
